# GLOSSARY — s15 Integrated Harness

Domain terms as used across `README.md`, `ARCHITECTURE.md`, and `code.py`
docstrings/comments. Every definition is grounded in the cited file and
function; entries are in alphabetical order.

### Active request

The running user request that the lead loop tracks as first-class state
(`session_state["active_user_request"]` in `__main__`, passed as
`active_request` through `agent_loop` in `code.py`). Scheduled cron lines
("Run scheduled task: …") are appended to it when jobs fire, and it is what
`compact_history` / `reactive_compact` preserve as the **Authoritative
request** field — the only field allowed to carry instructions after
compaction.

### Agent loop (integrated loop)

The single control loop shared by every lead turn, `agent_loop` in `code.py`:
inject scheduled cron prompts and background notifications, emit a todo
reminder, run the compaction pipeline (`prepare_context`), refresh context and
tool pool, call the model, then either stop (no concrete `tool_use` block —
checked by `has_tool_use`, not `stop_reason` alone) or dispatch the requested
tools and append their results as one user message, repeating.

### Async event loop

`async_event_loop` in `code.py`: the daemon thread ("lead-events") that polls
every second and, when the cron queue has fired, the lead's inbox has team
events, or background work finished, wakes the lead agent by running the same
`agent_loop` inside `traced_lead_turn` with a combined trigger
("cron+team+background").

### Background task

A `bash` call with `run_in_background: true` (`should_run_background`,
`start_background_task` in `code.py`) is moved into a daemon worker thread
(`background-<id>`, own process session); the model immediately receives a
placeholder tool_result, and the real output arrives later as a
`<task_notification>` user message via `collect_background_results` /
`inject_background_notifications` / `build_user_content`.

### Compaction

The layered, cheap-first context-shrinking pipeline in `prepare_context`
(`code.py`): `tool_result_budget` (persist oversized tool outputs of the
latest message to `.task_outputs/tool-results/`), `snip_compact` (archive old
message ranges to `.transcripts/`, keep head 3 + tail 46), `micro_compact`
(oldest consumed tool results → saved-path markers, keep the 3 newest),
`fit_tool_results` (largest results → 1000-char persisted previews), and
`compact_history` (full model summarization into one `[Compacted]` message) —
the last firing only while the estimated size (`estimate_size`,
`len(json.dumps(...))`) still exceeds `CONTEXT_LIMIT` (50000 chars). Two
additional entry points exist: the `compact` tool (special-cased in
`agent_loop`) and `reactive_compact` on prompt-too-long errors (at most once
per turn).

### Cron job

A scheduled prompt — a 5-field cron expression plus prompt, stored apart from
conversation history (`CronJob`, `schedule_job`, `validate_cron` in
`code.py`). A daemon scheduler thread (`cron_scheduler_loop`) ticks each
second and enqueues due jobs (deduped by a per-minute `_last_fired` marker);
`agent_loop` then consumes the queue as `[Scheduled]` user messages.
`durable` jobs persist to `.scheduled_tasks.json`, and one-shot jobs use
`pending_delivery` with `acknowledge_cron_jobs` / `restore_cron_jobs` for
at-least-once delivery.

### Error recovery

`RecoveryState` + `with_retry` in `code.py` wrap every model call with up to
3 attempts: 429/529 errors are retried with exponential backoff (500 ms base,
×2 per attempt, capped at 32 s, up to 25% jitter), and 2 consecutive 529s
switch to `FALLBACK_MODEL_ID` if configured. Separately, `agent_loop` recovers
`max_tokens` stops (one 8000→16000 escalation, then up to 2 continuation
prompts) and prompt-too-long errors (one-time `reactive_compact`, detected by
`is_prompt_too_long_error`).

### Harness decision

The `harness_decision` trace event emitted by `agent_loop` in `code.py` at
every control-flow branch — `dispatch_tools`, `continue` (reasons
`prompt_too_long`, `max_tokens`, `compact_tool`), and `stop` (reasons
`no_tool_use`, `model_error`, exhausted recovery) — carrying
`decision`/`reason`/`action` so a trace is a faithful record of the loop's
control flow.

### Hook

Extension points kept deliberately outside the tool handlers: the `HOOKS`
registry with `UserPromptSubmit`, `PreToolUse`, `PostToolUse`, and `Stop`
events, registered via `register_hook` and run by `trigger_hooks` in
`code.py`. `trigger_hooks` executes callbacks in registration order and
returns the first non-`None` result — for `PreToolUse` that string becomes the
denying tool_result. Built-ins: `user_prompt_hook`, `permission_hook` +
`log_hook` (PreToolUse), `large_output_hook` (PostToolUse, warns above 100000
chars), and `stop_hook` (counts tool results).

### Integrated harness

The s15 runtime as a whole (`code.py`, module docstring and `__main__`): one
Python process that combines the course's mechanisms — tool dispatch,
permissions/hooks, todo and task board, teams, worktrees, MCP, compaction,
background and cron, memory and skills, and tracing — into a single runnable
CLI agent sharing one `agent_loop`, one (traced) Anthropic client, and
file-backed state under the working directory.

### Lead agent

The interactive console agent (`agent-root`) running on the main thread
(`agent_loop`, `__main__` in `code.py`). It is the only thread allowed to ask
interactive permission questions — `permission_hook` fails closed for any
other thread — and it runs lead turns from user input or from the async event
loop while coordinating teammates.

### MCP integration

Late-bound external tools (`MCPClient`, `connect_mcp`, `assemble_tool_pool`,
`MCP_HOST_POLICY` in `code.py`): `connect_mcp` registers a server (in-process
mocks stand in for real MCP transports), and `assemble_tool_pool` merges its
tools into the pool under normalized `mcp__{server}__{tool}` names with
collision detection. Authorization comes from the host policy table
(default `confirm`), never from server-provided descriptions, and
`MCPClient.call_tool` bounds exceptions to `MCP error: …` strings.

### Memory runtime

The s09 memory runtime loaded by file path in `load_memory_runtime` (`code.py`),
sharing the host's client, model, and workspace (`.memory/`, index
`.memory/MEMORY.md`). Each turn `update_context` calls `load_memories`
(traced as purpose `memory_recall`) to supply the memory catalog and relevant
records for prompt assembly; at turn end `remember_after_turn` runs
`extract_memories` and, when new records are stored, `consolidate_memories`.

### One-shot subagent

The `task` tool (`spawn_subagent`, `SUB_SYSTEM` in `code.py`): a synchronous
nested tool loop (up to 30 rounds, five filesystem tools only) with an
isolated `messages[]` and its own system prompt, returning only the last
assistant text to the parent. It is traced as `agent_create` /
`agent_start` … `agent_end` with `agent_kind="one_shot"`.

### Permission boundary

Layered authorization checked on the raw `tool_use` block before dispatch
(`permission_hook`, `DENY_LIST`, `safe_path` in `code.py`): `bash` commands
are screened against a substring deny list (`rm -rf /`, `sudo`, …) and then
require an interactive `Allow? [y/N]` answer (main thread only — asynchronous
turns fail closed); `read_file`/`write_file`/`edit_file` paths must resolve
inside `WORKDIR`; `mcp__*` tools follow their host policy. A string returned
by the PreToolUse hook short-circuits dispatch and becomes the denying
tool_result.

### Plan gate

Per-teammate approval state (`plan_gates`, manipulated by
`spawn_teammate_thread`, `_teammate_submit_plan`, `_run_teammate_tool`,
`complete_task`, and `advance_assignment_version` in `code.py`): values
`required`/`pending`/`approved`/`rejected`/`not_required` hard-block
`bash`, `write_file`, and `edit_file` (in `_run_teammate_tool`) and
`complete_task` until the lead approves a submitted plan.
`advance_assignment_version` re-arms the gate to `required` whenever a new
assignment is claimed, so old approvals never leak into new work.

### Prompt assembly

`assemble_system_prompt` + `PROMPT_SECTIONS` in `code.py`: the system prompt
is rebuilt from live context **every turn** in fixed section order
(identity, tools, tasks, teams, workspace, memory, compaction), followed by
the current time, the skills catalog, and — when present — the memory
catalog, relevant memory records, and connected MCP servers, joined by blank
lines.

### Skill catalog

`skills/<name>/SKILL.md` packages (YAML frontmatter `name`/`description`)
scanned at startup into `SKILL_REGISTRY` by `scan_skills` (`code.py`). Only
the name-plus-description catalog (`list_skills`) enters the system prompt;
full skill content is fetched on demand through the `load_skill` tool.

### Summary stats

`trace_stats.py` (`validate_file`, `Aggregate.add_file`, `main`): a
read-only, directory-wide consumer of `traces/*.jsonl` that first validates
every line against the trace envelope (required fields, string `event`,
object `data`; warnings for schema drift, `run_id` changes, missing
`run_start`/`run_end`), then aggregates model calls/models, stop reasons,
token totals from `model_response` usage, tool-name frequency, and
error/retry counts. Exit code 1 if any malformed line is found.

### Task board

Cross-session, dependency-aware task records under `.tasks/task_*.json`
(`Task`, `create_task`, `update_task`, `claim_task`, `complete_task` in
`code.py`), protected by an in-process `RLock` plus a cross-process `flock`
and atomic tmp+rename writes. `update_task` adds `blockedBy` edges only while
a task is pending and unowned (rejecting self-dependencies, missing targets,
and cycles via `_task_depends_on`); `claim_task` atomically verifies all
blockers (`can_start`), sets the owner and `in_progress`, and binds the
owner's cwd lease; `complete_task` requires ownership and a cleared plan gate.

### Teammate

A persistent teammate agent in its own daemon thread (`teammate-<name>`,
created by `spawn_teammate_thread` in `code.py`) with a reduced tool pool
(five filesystem tools plus `send_message`, `submit_plan`, `list_tasks`,
`claim_task`, `complete_task`) and a `MessageBus` inbox. Its filesystem tools
resolve cwd through `assignment_cwd` and fail closed until a task is claimed;
its final text is delivered to the lead as a `result` message, and when idle
it waits on the bus before auto-claiming the next ready task via
`claim_next_task`.

### Tool dispatch

The per-`tool_use`-block sequence in `agent_loop` (`code.py`): the `compact`
special case, then `PreToolUse` hooks (which can deny), then background
dispatch for marked bash calls, then the handler inside a
`tool_execution_start`/`tool_execution_end` span via `call_tool_handler`,
followed by `PostToolUse` hooks. All results — plus any newly finished
background notifications — are collected and appended as a single user
message by `build_user_content`.

### Trace event

One JSON object per line in a `traces/run_*.jsonl` file, emitted by
`TraceRecorder.emit` in `trace_runtime.py` with a fixed envelope: schema
version 1.0, UTC timestamp, `monotonic_ns`, `elapsed_ms`, `run_id`, `turn_id`,
`event_id`, `event`, agent identity fields, `span_id`/`parent_span_id`,
causal fields, thread info, and redacted `data`. The file is opened mode 0600,
appended line-buffered, and flushed per event; harness examples include
`harness_decision`, `context_compact`, `cron_*`, `task_*`, `background_*`, and
`model_retry`.

### Trace runtime

The harness-independent tracing library in `trace_runtime.py`
(`BaseTraceRecorder`, `NullTraceRecorder`, `TraceRecorder`,
`create_recorder`, `TracedClient`) plus `initialize_tracing` in `code.py`:
`NullTraceRecorder` is the default so importing the lesson never creates
files, while the CLI entry point creates a `TraceRecorder` from the
`HARNESS_TRACE*` environment variables. `wrap_client` turns every
`messages.create` into a `model_request` → `model_response`/`model_error`
span; `contextvars` scopes (turn, agent, model purpose, span) with
`capture_context`/`restore_context` keep worker-thread events attributable;
and `span()` pairs start/end events by `span_id`, recording `duration_ms` and
capturing exceptions as error data.

### Worktree (task-bound)

A real Git worktree under `.worktrees/<name>` on branch `wt/<name>`, bound to
exactly one pending, unowned task after name, Git, and registry validation
(`create_worktree` in `code.py`). Claiming that task makes the worktree the
owner's cwd — `assignment_cwd`/`task_worktree_cwd` fail closed on broken
bindings — and removal stays host-owned (`remove_worktree`): it requires a
completed bound task, no active cwd leases or running background commands, and
a clean tree, and it always retains the branch.

# A Beginner's Tour of the s15 Integrated Harness
### Every glossary term, explained and demonstrated

Welcome! This tutorial teaches every term defined in `s15_integrated_harness/GLOSSARY.md` — all 25 of them — in plain language, each with its own worked example. Everything here is grounded in that glossary alone; you need no other background than "an AI coding agent is a program where a language model calls tools in a loop."

**Our running story.** Imagine you have just launched a coding agent in your project folder. Over one afternoon you will: chat with it while it reads and edits files, let it run a test suite in the background, schedule a daily morning summary, hire a helper agent to fix a bug in an isolated copy of your repo, and finally inspect its logs to see exactly what happened.

**Why this order?** The glossary lists terms alphabetically. I teach them in *story order* instead, because several terms only make sense after others: you cannot understand *hooks* before *tool dispatch*, or the *plan gate* before *teammates*. So we go: the whole system (Part 1), how a single turn works (Part 2), how the conversation stays manageable (Part 3), how work happens off the main thread and on a schedule (Part 4), how agents collaborate (Part 5), how the agent extends itself (Part 6), and how everything is observed (Part 7). Every term is defined before it is relied upon; where I must mention a later term early, I flag it.

---

## Part 1 — The big picture

### 1. Integrated harness

The **integrated harness** is the whole system: one Python process that combines the course's mechanisms — tool dispatch, permissions/hooks, a todo and task board, teams, worktrees, MCP, compaction, background tasks and cron jobs, memory and skills, and tracing — into a single runnable CLI agent. Everything shares one control loop (the *agent loop*, defined next), one traced Anthropic client, and file-backed state kept under the working directory.

**Worked example.** From your project folder you run:

```
$ python -m integrated_harness
agent-root> What can you do?
```

That one process now owns everything about your session: task records live in `.tasks/`, schedules in `.scheduled_tasks.json`, saved tool outputs in `.task_outputs/`, archived transcripts in `.transcripts/`, memories in `.memory/`, and logs in `traces/` — all inside this working directory. Close the process and those files remain; reopen it and the state is back.

### 2. Lead agent

The **lead agent** is the interactive console agent, internally named `agent-root`, running on the main thread. It is the boss of the session: it answers you directly, and it coordinates teammates (Part 5). Crucially, it is the *only* thread allowed to ask you interactive permission questions — the permission hook "fails closed" (refuses) for any other thread, so nothing but the lead can ever prompt you at the terminal.

**Worked example.** You type "Fix the failing test" at the console. That conversation *is* the lead. Ten minutes later, a teammate thread wants to run a shell command. You are not looking at any teammate terminal — teammates have none — so the permission hook denies the request automatically. The only path to an interactive "Allow? [y/N]" prompt is through the lead, i.e., through you.

### 3. Agent loop (integrated loop)

The **agent loop** is the single control loop shared by *every* lead turn. Each pass through it: (1) inject any due scheduled cron prompts and finished background notifications, (2) emit a todo reminder, (3) run the compaction pipeline (`prepare_context`) to keep the conversation within limits (Part 3), (4) refresh the context and the tool pool (the list of tools the model may call), (5) call the model, and then (6) either stop, or dispatch the requested tools and append their results as one user message — and go around again. "Stop" means the model produced *no concrete `tool_use` block*; the loop checks for an actual tool call (`has_tool_use`), not just the API's `stop_reason` label.

**Worked example.** You ask: "How many lines is main.py?"
- Pass 1: no cron jobs, no background results; `prepare_context` runs; the model returns a `tool_use` block for `bash wc -l main.py`. `has_tool_use` finds it, so the loop dispatches the command, appends the result (`42 main.py`) as one user message, and loops.
- Pass 2: the model answers with plain text — "main.py has 42 lines." No `tool_use` block exists, so the loop stops and you see the answer.

That two-pass rhythm — tool call, result, final answer — is the loop's heartbeat.

---

## Part 2 — How a single turn stays safe

### 4. Tool dispatch

**Tool dispatch** is the exact sequence the loop follows for each `tool_use` block the model requests. In order: the `compact` tool is special-cased first; then `PreToolUse` hooks run (they may deny the call — see term 6); then, if a bash call is marked to run in the background, it is dispatched that way instead (term 13); otherwise the tool's handler runs inside a `tool_execution_start`/`tool_execution_end` span via `call_tool_handler`; finally `PostToolUse` hooks run. All results — plus any background notifications that finished meanwhile — are gathered and appended as a *single* user message by `build_user_content`.

**Worked example.** The model requests two tools in one turn: `read_file notes.txt` and `bash pytest`. Dispatch handles each block in order: the compact special-case does not apply; PreToolUse hooks stay silent; pytest is not background-marked; `read_file` executes between its start/end spans; PostToolUse hooks observe it; the same treatment repeats for `bash`. You then see one combined user message carrying both results enter the transcript.

### 5. Permission boundary

The **permission boundary** is layered authorization checked on the raw `tool_use` block *before* dispatch. Layer 1: `bash` commands are screened against a substring deny list (`rm -rf /`, `sudo`, …). Layer 2: bash that survives the deny list needs an interactive `Allow? [y/N]` — main thread only, so asynchronous turns fail closed. Layer 3: `read_file`/`write_file`/`edit_file` paths must resolve inside `WORKDIR` (`safe_path`). Layer 4: `mcp__*` tools follow their host policy (term 20). A denying string from a PreToolUse hook short-circuits everything and becomes the `tool_result` the model sees.

**Worked example.** Three attempts in a row:
1. `bash sudo apt install fizz` → the deny list catches `sudo`; denied, no question asked.
2. `bash npm test` → you are shown `Allow? [y/N]`; you type `y`; it runs.
3. `write_file /etc/hosts` → `safe_path` resolves that outside `WORKDIR`; denied.

### 6. Hook

A **hook** is an extension point kept deliberately outside the tool handlers. The `HOOKS` registry supports four events — `UserPromptSubmit`, `PreToolUse`, `PostToolUse`, and `Stop` — registered with `register_hook` and run by `trigger_hooks`, which executes callbacks in registration order and returns the first non-`None` result. For `PreToolUse`, that returned string becomes the *denying* `tool_result`. Built-ins include `user_prompt_hook`; `permission_hook` plus `log_hook` (PreToolUse); `large_output_hook` (PostToolUse, warns above 100,000 characters); and `stop_hook`, which counts tool results.

**Worked example.** Your team freezes deploys on Fridays, so you write a ten-line function that returns "Deployments are frozen on Fridays" when it sees `bash deploy.sh`, and call `register_hook("PreToolUse", my_hook)`. On Friday the model calls `bash deploy.sh`; `trigger_hooks` walks the registry, your hook returns its string, and that string is delivered as the tool result. The command never executed — the model just reads the refusal and changes course.

---

## Part 3 — Keeping the conversation manageable

### 7. Prompt assembly

**Prompt assembly** (`assemble_system_prompt` + `PROMPT_SECTIONS`) builds the system prompt — the standing instructions the model reads before your conversation — and it is rebuilt from live context *every turn*, in fixed section order: identity, tools, tasks, teams, workspace, memory, compaction. After the sections come the current time, the skills catalog (term 23), and — when present — the memory catalog, relevant memory records, and connected MCP servers, all joined by blank lines.

**Worked example.** On turn 1, with no tasks, teammates, or memories yet, the prompt contains just identity, tools, and workspace sections plus the time and skill catalog. You then create a task on the board and connect a weather MCP server. On turn 2 the prompt is rebuilt from scratch and now also carries the tasks section and the MCP server list. Nothing stale is cached — the model always sees the current state of the world.

### 8. Active request

The **active request** is the running user request the lead loop tracks as first-class state (`session_state["active_user_request"]`, passed as `active_request` through `agent_loop`). When a scheduled cron job fires, its "Run scheduled task: …" line is appended to it. Most importantly, the compaction machinery (next term) always preserves it as the **Authoritative request** field — the only field allowed to carry instructions after compaction.

**Worked example.** You said "Build a snake game." Forty turns later the history must be compacted. The one `[Compacted]` summary message still contains, verbatim: `Authoritative request: Build a snake game`. Meanwhile a cron wanted "Summarize yesterday's commits" — that arrived as an appended scheduled line, but it can't hijack the goal: the authoritative field keeps the agent building the game.

### 9. Compaction

**Compaction** is the layered, cheapest-first pipeline (`prepare_context`) that shrinks the conversation: `tool_result_budget` persists oversized tool outputs of the latest message to `.task_outputs/tool-results/`; `snip_compact` archives old message ranges to `.transcripts/`, keeping the head 3 and tail 46 messages; `micro_compact` replaces the oldest already-consumed tool results with saved-path markers, keeping the 3 newest; `fit_tool_results` cuts the largest results to 1,000-character persisted previews; and only if the estimated size (`estimate_size`, i.e. `len(json.dumps(...))`) still exceeds `CONTEXT_LIMIT` (50,000 characters) does `compact_history` run full model summarization into one `[Compacted]` message. Two side doors exist: the `compact` tool (special-cased in the agent loop) and `reactive_compact`, fired at most once per turn on prompt-too-long errors.

**Worked example.** Your session hits 52,000 estimated characters — over the 50,000 limit. Step by step the cheap passes run: a 400 KB test log from the latest message is saved to `.task_outputs/tool-results/` with a pointer left behind; snipping archives turns 4–40 to `.transcripts/` keeping the first 3 and last 46; `micro_compact` replaces old tool results with saved-path markers; `fit_tool_results` trims the biggest remaining outputs to previews. Estimate now 31,000 — under the limit — so expensive `compact_history` never fires and no model-summarized `[Compacted]` message is needed.

### 10. Error recovery

**Error recovery** has two halves. Around every model call, `RecoveryState` + `with_retry` allow up to 3 attempts: 429/529 (overloaded/rate-limit) errors are retried with exponential backoff — 500 ms base, ×2 per attempt, capped at 32 s, with up to 25% jitter — and two consecutive 529s switch to `FALLBACK_MODEL_ID` if one is configured. Separately, the agent loop itself recovers from `max_tokens` stops (one 8000→16000 escalation, then up to 2 continuation prompts) and from prompt-too-long errors (a one-time `reactive_compact`, detected by `is_prompt_too_long_error`).

**Worked example.** The API returns 429 at 12:00:00; the call retries at ~12:00:00.5, fails again, retries at ~12:00:01.5 (jitter makes times inexact), succeeds — no user-visible error, just a `model_retry` trace line. Later, a huge answer hits `max_tokens`: the loop escalates max_tokens from 8000 to 16000 and asks the model to continue, stitching the answer together. And when a monster context triggers a prompt-too-long error, `is_prompt_too_long_error` spots it and `reactive_compact` shrinks the history once before retrying.

---

## Part 4 — Off-thread and on-schedule work

### 11. Background task

A **background task** is a `bash` call with `run_in_background: true`. Instead of making the model wait, `should_run_background`/`start_background_task` move it into a daemon worker thread (`background-<id>`, in its own process session); the model *immediately* receives a placeholder `tool_result` ("started"), and the real output arrives later as a `<task-notification>` user message, delivered via `collect_background_results` / `inject_background_notifications` / `build_user_content`.

**Worked example.** The model marks `npm test` as background. It instantly gets a placeholder like `task bg_1 started`, so it can reply "Tests are running; meanwhile I'll draft the README." Four minutes later the suite finishes, and a `<task-notification>` message — exit code, output tail — is injected into the conversation, waking the loop to report "All 58 tests passed."

### 12. Cron job

A **cron job** is a scheduled prompt: a 5-field cron expression (minute, hour, day-of-month, month, weekday) plus a prompt, stored *apart* from conversation history (`CronJob`, `schedule_job`, `validate_cron`). A daemon scheduler thread (`cron_scheduler_loop`) ticks every second and enqueues due jobs — deduplicated by a per-minute `_last_fired` marker. The agent loop then consumes the queue as `[Scheduled]` user messages. `durable` jobs persist to `.scheduled_tasks.json`; one-shot jobs use `pending_delivery` with `acknowledge_cron_jobs`/`restore_cron_jobs` for at-least-once delivery.

**Worked example.** You schedule `0 9 * * *` with prompt "Summarize open tasks." At 9:00:00 sharp the scheduler enqueues it (once — the `_last_fired` marker stops double-fires within the same minute), and your next turn begins with `[Scheduled] Run scheduled task: Summarize open tasks`. Because it was durable, a restart at 8:55 doesn't lose it — it's reloaded from `.scheduled_tasks.json`. A one-shot job that fires while the process is down is restored and delivered after restart, then acknowledged.

### 13. Async event loop

The **async event loop** (`async_event_loop`) is a daemon thread named "lead-events" that polls every second. When any of three things is pending — the cron queue has fired, the lead's inbox has team events, or background work finished — it wakes the lead agent by running the *same* agent loop inside `traced_lead_turn`, with a combined trigger string like "cron+team+background".

**Worked example.** You've stepped away from the keyboard. Within the same second: a teammate finishes its task (a team event), a background build completes, and a cron job fires. Instead of three separate wake-ups, "lead-events" notices all three pending sources and starts *one* lead turn with trigger `cron+team+background`, so all three updates are handled in a single pass.

---

## Part 5 — Agents working together

### 14. Task board

The **task board** is a set of cross-session, dependency-aware task records stored as `.tasks/task_*.json` files (`Task`, `create_task`, `update_task`, `claim_task`, `complete_task`), protected by an in-process `RLock` plus a cross-process `flock`, written atomically via tmp-file-then-rename. `update_task` adds `blockedBy` edges only while a task is pending and unowned, rejecting self-dependencies, missing targets, and cycles (`_task_depends_on`). `claim_task` atomically verifies all blockers (`can_start`), sets the owner and `in_progress`, and binds the owner's cwd lease. `complete_task` requires ownership and a cleared plan gate (term 16).

**Worked example.** You create `task_1 "install deps"` and `task_2 "run migration"` blocked by `task_1`. A teammate tries to make `task_2` block itself → rejected. Another tries `claim_task task_2` → `can_start` fails, because `task_1` isn't complete. After `task_1` is completed, the claim succeeds: the JSON file is atomically rewritten with `owner: "builder"`, `status: in_progress`, and builder's cwd lease recorded.

### 15. Teammate

A **teammate** is a persistent teammate agent living in its own daemon thread (`teammate-<name>`, created by `spawn_teammate_thread`) with a reduced tool pool — the five filesystem tools plus `send_message`, `submit_plan`, `list_tasks`, `claim_task`, and `complete_task` — and a `MessageBus` inbox. Its filesystem tools resolve the working directory through `assignment_cwd` and fail closed until it has claimed a task. Its final text is delivered to the lead as a `result` message, and when idle it waits on the bus before auto-claiming the next ready task via `claim_next_task`.

**Worked example.** You spawn a teammate called `builder`. Its first `read_file` fails closed — no task claimed yet. It lists the board, claims `task_2 "fix login bug"`, and suddenly its file tools work, resolved inside the assignment cwd. It messages you progress (`send_message`), and finishes with a final text that lands in your lead conversation as a `result` message. Rather than exiting, it idles on the bus — and when you add `task_3`, it auto-claims it via `claim_next_task`.

### 16. Plan gate

The **plan gate** is per-teammate approval state (`plan_gates`), with values `required`, `pending`, `approved`, `rejected`, or `not_required`. While the gate is unsatisfied, `_run_teammate_tool` hard-blocks `bash`, `write_file`, and `edit_file`, and `complete_task` is also blocked — until the lead approves a submitted plan. When `advance_assignment_version` runs because the teammate claimed a *new* assignment, the gate re-arms to `required`, so old approvals never leak into new work.

**Worked example.** `builder` starts a task with the gate at `required` and calls `write_file` → blocked. It calls `submit_plan("update auth.py; add one test")` → gate becomes `pending`. You approve → `approved` → the same `write_file` now goes through, and later `complete_task` succeeds. `builder` claims its next task: the gate snaps back to `required` — yesterday's approval doesn't cover today's work.

### 17. One-shot subagent

A **one-shot subagent** is the `task` tool (`spawn_subagent`, with its own `SUB_SYSTEM` prompt): a synchronous *nested* tool loop — up to 30 rounds, five filesystem tools only — with an isolated `messages[]` history. It returns only its last assistant text to the parent, and it is traced as `agent_create` / `agent_start` … `agent_end` with `agent_kind="one_shot"`.

**Worked example.** You ask the lead: "Count TODO comments under src/." Instead of littering your transcript with 40 tool calls, the lead calls `task` with that instruction. A subagent spins up its own little loop — grep, read, tally, up to 30 rounds — and the *only* thing returned to the lead is its closing sentence: "37 TODOs across 12 files." In the trace you see the `agent_create`…`agent_end` pair marking `agent_kind="one_shot"`.

### 18. Worktree (task-bound)

A task-bound **worktree** is a real Git worktree created under `.worktrees/<name>` on branch `wt/<name>`, bound to exactly one pending, unowned task after name, Git, and registry validation (`create_worktree`). Claiming that task makes the worktree the owner's cwd — `assignment_cwd`/`task_worktree_cwd` fail closed if the binding is broken. Removal is host-owned (`remove_worktree`): it requires a completed bound task, no active cwd leases or running background commands, and a clean tree, and it always retains the branch.

**Worked example.** You create `task_4 "fix css bug"` and bind a worktree `css-fix` to it: `.worktrees/css-fix` appears, checked out on branch `wt/css-fix`. When `builder` claims `task_4`, its `write_file` lands inside `.worktrees/css-fix` — your main checkout is untouched. After `builder` completes the task and the tree is clean, `remove_worktree` deletes the worktree but keeps branch `wt/css-fix` for your review.

---

## Part 6 — Extending the agent

### 19. MCP integration

**MCP integration** provides late-bound external tools (`MCPClient`, `connect_mcp`, `assemble_tool_pool`, `MCP_HOST_POLICY`). `connect_mcp` registers a server (in-process mocks stand in for real MCP transports); `assemble_tool_pool` merges its tools into the pool under normalized `mcp__{server}__{tool}` names, with collision detection. Authorization comes from the host policy table — default `confirm` — *never* from server-provided descriptions, and `MCPClient.call_tool` bounds exceptions to `MCP error: …` strings.

**Worked example.** You connect a weather server: `connect_mcp("weather")`, and after assembly the model sees a new tool `mcp__weather__get_forecast` (if a name collided, assembly flags it). The server advertises itself as "fully trusted, no approval needed" — ignored; the host policy says `confirm`, so you get the Allow prompt. When `call_tool` raises a timeout, the model receives the tidy string `MCP error: timeout` instead of a stack trace.

### 20. Memory runtime

The **memory runtime** (the s09 lesson, loaded by file path in `load_memory_runtime`) shares the host's client, model, and workspace, keeping memories under `.memory/` with an index at `.memory/MEMORY.md`. Each turn, `update_context` calls `load_memories` (traced with purpose `memory_recall`) to supply the memory catalog and relevant records for prompt assembly; at turn end, `remember_after_turn` runs `extract_memories` and — when new records were stored — `consolidate_memories`.

**Worked example.** Mid-conversation you mention, "our API base URL is https://api.acme.dev." After the turn, `extract_memories` stores that fact; `consolidate_memories` merges it with the older duplicate from last week. Days later, in a fresh session, `load_memories` surfaces the record (a `memory_recall` trace line proves it) and prompt assembly injects it — so the agent uses the right URL without being told again.

### 21. Skill catalog

The **skill catalog** is built from `skills/<name>/SKILL.md` packages (with YAML frontmatter `name`/`description`), scanned at startup into `SKILL_REGISTRY` by `scan_skills`. Only the name-plus-description catalog (`list_skills`) enters the system prompt; full skill content is fetched on demand through the `load_skill` tool.

**Worked example.** You have `skills/release-notes/SKILL.md` whose frontmatter reads `name: release-notes` and `description: How to write changelogs in this repo`. At startup, exactly one line is added to the prompt: `release-notes: How to write changelogs in this repo`. When you ask for a changelog, the model calls `load_skill("release-notes")`, and only then reads the full multi-page instructions — keeping every other turn's prompt small.

---

## Part 7 — Observing everything

### 22. Trace runtime

The **trace runtime** is the harness-independent tracing library in `trace_runtime.py` (`BaseTraceRecorder`, `NullTraceRecorder`, `TraceRecorder`, `create_recorder`, `TracedClient`) plus `initialize_tracing` in `code.py`. `NullTraceRecorder` is the default, so merely importing the lesson never creates files; the CLI entry point creates a real `TraceRecorder` from `HARNESS_TRACE*` environment variables. `wrap_client` turns every `messages.create` into a `model_request` → `model_response` (or `model_error`) span; `contextvars` scopes (turn, agent, model purpose, span), carried across threads with `capture_context`/`restore_context`, keep worker-thread events attributable; and `span()` pairs start/end events by `span_id`, recording `duration_ms` and capturing exceptions as error data.

**Worked example.** In a unit test you import the module — with the default `NullTraceRecorder`, zero files appear. You then launch the CLI with `HARNESS_TRACE_DIR=traces`, and a real recorder comes alive. When a teammate thread calls the model, its events still carry the correct turn and agent identity, because `capture_context`/`restore_context` ferried the context across the thread boundary. An exception inside a span shows up as error data alongside its `duration_ms`.

### 23. Trace event

A **trace event** is one JSON object per line in a `traces/run_*.jsonl` file, emitted by `TraceRecorder.emit` with a fixed envelope: schema version 1.0, UTC timestamp, `monotonic_ns`, `elapsed_ms`, `run_id`, `turn_id`, `event_id`, the `event` name, agent identity fields, `span_id`/`parent_span_id`, causal fields, thread info, and redacted `data`. The file is opened mode 0600, appended line-buffered, and flushed per event. Typical harness events include `harness_decision`, `context_compact`, `cron_*`, `task_*`, `background_*`, and `model_retry`.

**Worked example.** One line from a real-looking run (pretty-printed here for readability):

```json
{"schema": "1.0", "ts": "2025-06-01T09:15:03.412Z", "elapsed_ms": 48213,
 "run_id": "run_007", "turn_id": 12, "event_id": 204, "event": "tool_execution_end",
 "agent": "agent-root", "span_id": "s9f2", "parent_span_id": "t12",
 "thread": "main", "data": {"tool": "read_file", "chars": 812}}
```

Six hundred such lines, flushed one per event in a 0600-permission file, are your session's black-box recorder.

### 24. Harness decision

A **harness decision** is the trace event the agent loop emits at *every* control-flow branch: `dispatch_tools` (tools will run), `continue` (reasons: `prompt_too_long`, `max_tokens`, `compact_tool`), or `stop` (reasons: `no_tool_use`, `model_error`, exhausted recovery). Each event carries `decision`/`reason`/`action`, so a trace is a faithful record of the loop's control flow — you can reconstruct *why* it did what it did without reading any code.

**Worked example.** Three lines tell a whole story:

```
event=harness_decision decision=continue        reason=prompt_too_long action=reactive_compact
event=harness_decision decision=dispatch_tools  reason=tool_use         action=bash pytest
event=harness_decision decision=stop            reason=no_tool_use      action=end_turn
```

Reading them top to bottom: the context overflowed and was compacted, the model then requested `pytest` and the loop dispatched it, and finally the model answered in plain text so the loop stopped.

### 25. Summary stats

**Summary stats** (`trace_stats.py`, with `validate_file`, `Aggregate.add_file`, and `main`) is a read-only, directory-wide consumer of `traces/*.jsonl`. It first validates every line against the trace envelope (required fields present, `event` a string, `data` an object; warnings for schema drift, `run_id` changes, missing `run_start`/`run_end`), then aggregates model calls and models, stop reasons, token totals from `model_response` usage, tool-name frequency, and error/retry counts. Exit code is 1 if any malformed line is found.

**Worked example.** You run:

```
$ python trace_stats.py traces/
model calls: 214  models: claude-sonnet=210, fallback=4
stop reasons: end_turn=180, max_tokens=34
tokens: in=412,330  out=61,208
top tools: read_file=57, bash=41, write_file=22
retries: 3   errors: 1
WARNING run_003.jsonl line 417: event is not a string
$ echo $?
1
```

One warning, exit code 1: the run summary is useful *and* the malformed line cannot slip past silently.

---

## Wrap-up

You have now met all 25 glossary terms in story order: the **integrated harness** and its **lead agent**; the **agent loop** with **tool dispatch**, the **permission boundary**, and **hooks**; **prompt assembly**, the **active request**, **compaction**, and **error recovery**; **background tasks**, **cron jobs**, and the **async event loop**; the **task board**, **teammates**, **plan gates**, **one-shot subagents**, and task-bound **worktrees**; **MCP integration**, the **memory runtime**, and the **skill catalog**; and finally the observability trio of **trace runtime**, **trace events**, **harness decisions**, and **summary stats**. Together they describe one process in which a model calls tools in a checked, recorded, recoverable loop — and now every word of that description is yours.

# The s15 Integrated Harness: A Beginner's Tutorial Through Every Glossary Term

## 1. Introduction: what is the "integrated harness"?

Imagine a plain language model sitting in a chat window. It can write text, but it cannot run commands, remember yesterday, or wake up on a schedule. The integrated harness is the missing machinery: one Python process (code.py) that combines the course's individual mechanisms - tool dispatch, permissions and hooks, a todo and task board, teams, Git worktrees, MCP, compaction, background tasks and cron jobs, memory and skills, and tracing - into a single runnable CLI agent. Everything shares one control loop (the agent loop), one traced Anthropic client, and file-backed state stored under your working directory.

Worked example: you cd into a small project called notes-app, run the harness, and type "tidy up this repository and add a README." Within one process, the request is remembered, tools are offered to the model, permissions are checked, the context is compacted when it grows, and every step is written to a trace file. The rest of this tutorial walks through each piece of that story, term by term.

## 2. The heart of the system: one loop

### Agent loop (integrated loop)

Every lead turn - no matter what triggered it - runs the same agent_loop. In order, it injects any scheduled cron prompts and background notifications into the conversation, emits a todo reminder, runs the compaction pipeline (prepare_context), refreshes the context and tool pool, calls the model, and then either stops or dispatches tools. The stop condition is precise: the loop stops only when the response contains no concrete tool_use block (checked by has_tool_use, not by stop_reason alone). Otherwise it dispatches the requested tools and appends their results as one user message, then repeats.

Worked example: you type "list the Python files here." The model replies with a tool_use block calling bash with ls *.py. The loop dispatches it, appends the output as one user message, calls the model again, and this time the model answers in plain prose. has_tool_use finds no tool call, so the loop stops and prints the answer.

### Lead agent

The lead agent (agent-root) is the interactive console agent running on the main thread. It is special in one crucial way: it is the only thread allowed to ask you interactive permission questions. The permission_hook deliberately fails closed for any other thread - a background thread can never pop an Allow? [y/N] prompt at you.

Worked example: the lead runs bash "rm old/" and you see Allow? [y/N] on the console and answer y. Later, a teammate thread tries the same command; because it is not the main thread, the permission hook refuses it automatically rather than prompting.

### Prompt assembly

Before each model call the harness rebuilds the entire system prompt from live context - every single turn - using assemble_system_prompt and PROMPT_SECTIONS. Sections always appear in fixed order: identity, tools, tasks, teams, workspace, memory, compaction. After them come the current time, the skills catalog, and - when present - the memory catalog, relevant memory records, and connected MCP servers, joined by blank lines.

Worked example: in turn 1 you have no tasks; in turn 2 you claim a task and connect an MCP weather server. The turn-2 system prompt is rebuilt from scratch and now contains a Tasks section and an MCP servers section, so the model instantly "knows" about both without any code change.

### Tool dispatch

When the model's reply contains tool calls, each tool_use block goes through a fixed dispatch sequence in agent_loop: first the compact special case; then PreToolUse hooks, which may deny the call; then background dispatch for bash calls marked run_in_background: true; then the actual handler runs inside a tool_execution_start / tool_execution_end span via call_tool_handler; and finally PostToolUse hooks run. Worked example: the model asks for two things at once - read_file NOTES.md and bash wc -l *.py. Each block passes through the sequence independently, and both results land together in one user message, ready for the model's next turn.

### Harness decision

Because the loop has several branches, it records its choices. At every control-flow branch agent_loop emits a harness_decision trace event carrying decision / reason / action: dispatch_tools, continue (reasons prompt_too_long, max_tokens, compact_tool), or stop (reasons no_tool_use, model_error, exhausted recovery). Worked example: after a session you open traces/run_0042.jsonl and find the final event harness_decision with decision="stop", reason="no_tool_use" - proof the run ended normally rather than through an error.

## 3. Guardrails: permissions, hooks, recovery

### Permission boundary

Authorization is layered and checked on the raw tool_use block before dispatch. First, bash commands are screened against a substring deny list (rm -rf /, sudo, ...) in DENY_LIST. Then bash still requires an interactive Allow? [y/N] answer - main thread only; asynchronous turns fail closed. Next, read_file / write_file / edit_file paths must resolve inside WORKDIR (safe_path), and mcp__* tools follow their host policy. A string returned by the PreToolUse hook short-circuits dispatch and becomes the denying tool_result.

Worked example: you ask the agent to bash "sudo apt install jq" - the deny list rejects it instantly, with no prompt. You then ask it to read_file /etc/passwd - the path resolves outside the working directory, so it is refused. Finally read_file README.md passes both layers and reaches your y/N prompt.

### Hook

Hooks are extension points kept deliberately outside the tool handlers. The HOOKS registry knows four events - UserPromptSubmit, PreToolUse, PostToolUse, Stop - registered via register_hook and run by trigger_hooks, which executes callbacks in registration order and returns the first non-None result. For PreToolUse, that returned string becomes the denying tool_result. Built-ins include user_prompt_hook; permission_hook and log_hook (PreToolUse); large_output_hook (PostToolUse, warns above 100000 chars); and stop_hook (counts tool results).

Worked example: you register a PreToolUse hook that returns "denied: never force-push" when a bash command contains git push --force. When the model later tries it, trigger_hooks returns that string, dispatch short-circuits, and the model sees the denial as its tool_result and picks a safer approach.

### Error recovery

Every model call is wrapped by RecoveryState and with_retry for up to 3 attempts: 429/529 errors are retried with exponential backoff (500 ms base, x2 per attempt, capped at 32 s, up to 25% jitter), and two consecutive 529s switch to FALLBACK_MODEL_ID if configured. Separately, the loop recovers max_tokens stops (one 8000 to 16000 escalation, then up to 2 continuation prompts) and prompt-too-long errors (a one-time reactive_compact, detected by is_prompt_too_long_error).

Worked example: the API returns 429 "rate limited." with_retry waits about 500 ms plus jitter, retries, and succeeds - a model_retry event lands in the trace. If a response is instead cut off by max_tokens, the loop raises the limit to 16000 and asks the model to continue where it left off.

### Plan gate

Teammates cannot just start editing. Each teammate has a per-teammate approval state in plan_gates with values required / pending / approved / rejected / not_required. While the gate is not approved, _run_teammate_tool hard-blocks bash, write_file, and edit_file, and complete_task is blocked too. When a new assignment is claimed, advance_assignment_version re-arms the gate to required, so old approvals never leak into new work.

Worked example: teammate alice tries write_file notes.txt before submitting a plan - blocked. She calls submit_plan with "create notes.txt listing cleanup steps." You, the lead, approve, and the identical write now succeeds.

## 4. Working across time

### Background task

Long-running shell work does not have to block the conversation. A bash call with run_in_background: true is moved by should_run_background and start_background_task into a daemon worker thread named background-<id> with its own process session. The model immediately receives a placeholder tool_result, and the real output arrives later as a <task_notification> user message, assembled by collect_background_results, inject_background_notifications, and build_user_content.

Worked example: the model starts your test suite with run_in_background: true and instantly gets "started in background, id 7." It goes on writing documentation; two turns later a <task_notification> arrives: "task 7 finished: 41 passed."

### Async event loop

Who wakes the agent when you have typed nothing for ten minutes? The async_event_loop, a daemon thread named "lead-events," polls every second. When the cron queue has fired, the lead's inbox has team events, or background work has finished, it wakes the lead agent by running the same agent_loop inside traced_lead_turn with a combined trigger: "cron+team+background".

Worked example: you leave the terminal open and go to lunch. A cron job fires at 12:00; the lead-events thread notices, wakes the lead with trigger "cron+team+background", and by the time you return, the harness has already run and summarized the scheduled check.

### Cron job

A cron job is a scheduled prompt: a 5-field cron expression plus a prompt, stored apart from conversation history (CronJob, schedule_job, validate_cron). A daemon scheduler thread (cron_scheduler_loop) ticks each second and enqueues due jobs, deduplicated by a per-minute _last_fired marker. agent_loop then consumes the queue as [Scheduled] user messages. Durable jobs persist to .scheduled_tasks.json, and one-shot jobs use pending_delivery with acknowledge_cron_jobs and restore_cron_jobs for at-least-once delivery.

Worked example: you say "every 5 minutes, check whether the dev server is up." The job with expression */5 * * * * is stored; at 12:05 the scheduler enqueues it, the loop injects "[Scheduled] Run scheduled task: check whether the dev server is up", and the model answers with a bash curl against localhost:8000.

Two more entry points exist: the compact tool (special-cased in agent_loop) and reactive_compact on prompt-too-long errors, at most once per turn.

Worked example: after an hour of refactoring, your history is 120,000 characters. First, old message ranges are archived to .transcripts/; if the size is still too big, stale tool results shrink to "saved to .task_outputs/..." markers; if it still exceeds 50000 characters, a model-written summary collapses it all into a single [Compacted] message.

Scheduled cron lines ("Run scheduled task: ...") are appended to it when jobs fire, and it is what compact_history and reactive_compact preserve as the Authoritative request field - the only field allowed to carry instructions after compaction.

Worked example: you asked "migrate config.ini to YAML," and the context has since been compacted twice. The short new history still begins with "Authoritative request: migrate config.ini to YAML," so the model finishes your original job instead of drifting into whatever the summary emphasized.

## 5. Delegation: subagents, teammates, tasks, worktrees

### One-shot subagent

The task tool (spawn_subagent, SUB_SYSTEM) creates a one-shot subagent: a synchronous nested tool loop (up to 30 rounds, five filesystem tools only) with an isolated messages[] and its own system prompt, returning only the last assistant text to the parent. Traces show agent_create, agent_start, and agent_end with agent_kind="one_shot".

Worked example: you ask "find every TODO comment in the repo and summarize the themes." The lead spawns a subagent that greps and reads for a while; the parent receives just the final paragraph - "12 TODOs, mostly about error handling" - with none of the intermediate noise.

### Teammate

A teammate is a persistent agent in its own daemon thread (teammate-<name>, created by spawn_teammate_thread) with a reduced tool pool - five filesystem tools plus send_message, submit_plan, list_tasks, claim_task, and complete_task - and a MessageBus inbox. Its filesystem tools resolve the working directory through assignment_cwd and fail closed until a task is claimed. Its final text is delivered to the lead as a result message, and when idle it waits on the bus before auto-claiming the next ready task via claim_next_task.

Worked example: you spawn "bob" and assign "write the README." Bob cannot read or write anything yet (fail closed), claims the task, and only now do his file tools resolve to the assignment directory. When he finishes, his final text lands in your transcript as a result message from bob.

Coordination runs through cross-session, dependency-aware task records under .tasks/task_*.json (Task, create_task, update_task, claim_task, complete_task), protected by an in-process RLock plus a cross-process flock, with atomic tmp+rename writes. update_task adds blockedBy edges only while a task is pending and unowned, rejecting self-dependencies, missing targets, and cycles (checked by _task_depends_on). claim_task atomically verifies all blockers (can_start), sets the owner and in_progress, and binds the owner's cwd lease; complete_task requires ownership and a cleared plan gate.

### Worktree (task-bound)

Experiments should not trample each other. A task-bound worktree is a real Git worktree under .worktrees/<name> on branch wt/<name>, bound to exactly one pending, unowned task after name, Git, and registry validation (create_worktree). Claiming that task makes the worktree the owner's cwd - assignment_cwd and task_worktree_cwd fail closed on broken bindings. Removal stays host-owned (remove_worktree): it requires a completed bound task, no active cwd leases or running background commands, and a clean tree, and it always retains the branch.

Worked example: task C "try Redis caching" is bound to worktree .worktrees/caching on branch wt/caching. When a teammate claims C, all her file edits happen inside that worktree; your main checkout is untouched. Later the host removes the worktree, but the branch survives for review.

### MCP integration

Worked example: you connect a "weather" server exposing get_forecast. The model now sees mcp__weather__get_forecast; on first use the host policy says confirm, so you approve it. ### Memory runtime

The harness remembers between sessions via the s09 memory runtime, loaded by file path in load_memory_runtime, sharing the host's client, model, and workspace (.memory/ with index .memory/MEMORY.md). Each turn, update_context calls load_memories (traced as purpose memory_recall) to supply the memory catalog and relevant records for prompt assembly; at turn end, remember_after_turn runs extract_memories and, when new records are stored, consolidate_memories.

Worked example: you mention once, "the staging database runs on port 5433." At turn end that fact is extracted and stored under .memory/. Next session, load_memories surfaces it in the prompt, and the model connects to 5433 without being told again.

### Skill catalog

Skills are reusable instruction packages: skills/<name>/SKILL.md files with YAML frontmatter (name and description), scanned at startup into SKILL_REGISTRY by scan_skills. Only the name-plus-description catalog (list_skills) enters the system prompt; full skill content is fetched on demand through the load_skill tool.

Worked example: you write skills/release-checklist/SKILL.md describing your release steps. Every turn the model sees only "release-checklist: steps for cutting a release"; when you say "do a release," it calls load_skill and finally reads the full checklist.

## 7. Seeing everything: tracing

### Trace runtime

Tracing is a harness-independent library in trace_runtime.py: BaseTraceRecorder, NullTraceRecorder, TraceRecorder, create_recorder, and TracedClient, plus initialize_tracing in code.py. NullTraceRecorder is the default, so merely importing the lesson never creates files; the CLI entry point creates a real TraceRecorder from the HARNESS_TRACE* environment variables. wrap_client turns every messages.create into a model_request to model_response or model_error span; contextvars scopes (turn, agent, model purpose, span) with capture_context and restore_context keep worker-thread events attributable; and span() pairs start/end events by span_id, recording duration_ms and capturing exceptions as error data.

Worked example: you export HARNESS_TRACE=1 and start the CLI; a traces/run_*.jsonl file appears (mode 0600). Inside, each model call is bracketed by model_request and model_response spans with a measured duration_ms, and events from teammate threads still carry the correct turn and agent ids thanks to the captured context.

### Trace event

One JSON object per line in a traces/run_*.jsonl file is a trace event, emitted by TraceRecorder.emit with a fixed envelope: schema version 1.0, UTC timestamp, monotonic_ns, elapsed_ms, run_id, turn_id, event_id, event, agent identity fields, span_id and parent_span_id, causal fields, thread info, and redacted data. The file is opened mode 0600, appended line-buffered, and flushed per event. Harness examples include harness_decision, context_compact, cron_*, task_*, background_*, and model_retry.

Worked example: after a flaky session you run grep model_retry traces/run_0007.jsonl and see three lines, each with a timestamp and backoff details - a compact, permanent record of exactly when the API rate-limited you and how the harness responded.

### Summary stats

trace_stats.py is a read-only, directory-wide consumer of traces/*.jsonl (validate_file, Aggregate.add_file, main). It first validates every line against the trace envelope (required fields, string event, object data; warnings for schema drift, run_id changes, missing run_start or run_end), then aggregates model calls and models, stop reasons, token totals from model_response usage, tool-name frequency, and error/retry counts. Exit code 1 if any malformed line is found.

Worked example: you run python trace_stats.py traces/ and get a report: 214 model calls across 2 models, 96 stops with reason no_tool_use, 8,412 tool calls with bash most frequent, 3 retries. Because you once hand-edited a line, the tool prints a warning and exits 1, telling you which file to fix.

## 8. Putting it all together

One story ties all 25 terms together. You start the integrated harness in notes-app (integrated harness) and type a goal, which becomes the active request. Each turn, the lead agent wakes through the agent loop; the system prompt is rebuilt by prompt assembly; the model calls tools that pass through tool dispatch under the permission boundary and hooks; failures are absorbed by error recovery; and each branch is recorded as a harness decision. Heavy shell work becomes a background task, while the async event loop and cron jobs wake the agent when you are away, and compaction - protecting the active request - keeps the context under the limit. Work is delegated to a one-shot subagent for research, and to teammates who plan through a plan gate, pull work from the task board, and edit safely inside a task-bound worktree. Capabilities grow through MCP integration, the memory runtime, and the skill catalog. And because every step emits a trace event through the trace runtime, summary stats can later prove what happened. Master these terms and you can read, predict, and debug the whole harness.

# GLOSSARY — s15 Integrated Harness

Domain terms as used across `README.md`, `ARCHITECTURE.md`, and `code.py`
docstrings/comments. Every definition is grounded in the cited file and
function; entries are in alphabetical order.

### Active request

The running user request that the lead loop tracks as first-class state
(`session_state["active_user_request"]` in `__main__`, passed as
`active_request` through `agent_loop` in `code.py`). Scheduled cron lines
("Run scheduled task: …") are appended to it when jobs fire, and it is what
`compact_history` / `reactive_compact` preserve as the **Authoritative
request** field — the only field allowed to carry instructions after
compaction.

### Agent loop (integrated loop)

The single control loop shared by every lead turn, `agent_loop` in `code.py`:
inject scheduled cron prompts and background notifications, emit a todo
reminder, run the compaction pipeline (`prepare_context`), refresh context and
tool pool, call the model, then either stop (no concrete `tool_use` block —
checked by `has_tool_use`, not `stop_reason` alone) or dispatch the requested
tools and append their results as one user message, repeating.

### Async event loop

`async_event_loop` in `code.py`: the daemon thread ("lead-events") that polls
every second and, when the cron queue has fired, the lead's inbox has team
events, or background work finished, wakes the lead agent by running the same
`agent_loop` inside `traced_lead_turn` with a combined trigger
("cron+team+background").

### Background task

A `bash` call with `run_in_background: true` (`should_run_background`,
`start_background_task` in `code.py`) is moved into a daemon worker thread
(`background-<id>`, own process session); the model immediately receives a
placeholder tool_result, and the real output arrives later as a
`<task_notification>` user message via `collect_background_results` /
`inject_background_notifications` / `build_user_content`.

### Compaction

The layered, cheap-first context-shrinking pipeline in `prepare_context`
(`code.py`): `tool_result_budget` (persist oversized tool outputs of the
latest message to `.task_outputs/tool-results/`), `snip_compact` (archive old
message ranges to `.transcripts/`, keep head 3 + tail 46), `micro_compact`
(oldest consumed tool results → saved-path markers, keep the 3 newest),
`fit_tool_results` (largest results → 1000-char persisted previews), and
`compact_history` (full model summarization into one `[Compacted]` message) —
the last firing only while the estimated size (`estimate_size`,
`len(json.dumps(...))`) still exceeds `CONTEXT_LIMIT` (50000 chars). Two
additional entry points exist: the `compact` tool (special-cased in
`agent_loop`) and `reactive_compact` on prompt-too-long errors (at most once
per turn).

### Cron job

A scheduled prompt — a 5-field cron expression plus prompt, stored apart from
conversation history (`CronJob`, `schedule_job`, `validate_cron` in
`code.py`). A daemon scheduler thread (`cron_scheduler_loop`) ticks each
second and enqueues due jobs (deduped by a per-minute `_last_fired` marker);
`agent_loop` then consumes the queue as `[Scheduled]` user messages.
`durable` jobs persist to `.scheduled_tasks.json`, and one-shot jobs use
`pending_delivery` with `acknowledge_cron_jobs` / `restore_cron_jobs` for
at-least-once delivery.

### Error recovery

`RecoveryState` + `with_retry` in `code.py` wrap every model call with up to
3 attempts: 429/529 errors are retried with exponential backoff (500 ms base,
×2 per attempt, capped at 32 s, up to 25% jitter), and 2 consecutive 529s
switch to `FALLBACK_MODEL_ID` if configured. Separately, `agent_loop` recovers
`max_tokens` stops (one 8000→16000 escalation, then up to 2 continuation
prompts) and prompt-too-long errors (one-time `reactive_compact`, detected by
`is_prompt_too_long_error`).

### Harness decision

The `harness_decision` trace event emitted by `agent_loop` in `code.py` at
every control-flow branch — `dispatch_tools`, `continue` (reasons
`prompt_too_long`, `max_tokens`, `compact_tool`), and `stop` (reasons
`no_tool_use`, `model_error`, exhausted recovery) — carrying
`decision`/`reason`/`action` so a trace is a faithful record of the loop's
control flow.

### Hook

Extension points kept deliberately outside the tool handlers: the `HOOKS`
registry with `UserPromptSubmit`, `PreToolUse`, `PostToolUse`, and `Stop`
events, registered via `register_hook` and run by `trigger_hooks` in
`code.py`. `trigger_hooks` executes callbacks in registration order and
returns the first non-`None` result — for `PreToolUse` that string becomes the
denying tool_result. Built-ins: `user_prompt_hook`, `permission_hook` +
`log_hook` (PreToolUse), `large_output_hook` (PostToolUse, warns above 100000
chars), and `stop_hook` (counts tool results).

### Integrated harness

The s15 runtime as a whole (`code.py`, module docstring and `__main__`): one
Python process that combines the course's mechanisms — tool dispatch,
permissions/hooks, todo and task board, teams, worktrees, MCP, compaction,
background and cron, memory and skills, and tracing — into a single runnable
CLI agent sharing one `agent_loop`, one (traced) Anthropic client, and
file-backed state under the working directory.

### Lead agent

The interactive console agent (`agent-root`) running on the main thread
(`agent_loop`, `__main__` in `code.py`). It is the only thread allowed to ask
interactive permission questions — `permission_hook` fails closed for any
other thread — and it runs lead turns from user input or from the async event
loop while coordinating teammates.

### MCP integration

Late-bound external tools (`MCPClient`, `connect_mcp`, `assemble_tool_pool`,
`MCP_HOST_POLICY` in `code.py`): `connect_mcp` registers a server (in-process
mocks stand in for real MCP transports), and `assemble_tool_pool` merges its
tools into the pool under normalized `mcp__{server}__{tool}` names with
collision detection. Authorization comes from the host policy table
(default `confirm`), never from server-provided descriptions, and
`MCPClient.call_tool` bounds exceptions to `MCP error: …` strings.

### Memory runtime

The s09 memory runtime loaded by file path in `load_memory_runtime` (`code.py`),
sharing the host's client, model, and workspace (`.memory/`, index
`.memory/MEMORY.md`). Each turn `update_context` calls `load_memories`
(traced as purpose `memory_recall`) to supply the memory catalog and relevant
records for prompt assembly; at turn end `remember_after_turn` runs
`extract_memories` and, when new records are stored, `consolidate_memories`.

### One-shot subagent

The `task` tool (`spawn_subagent`, `SUB_SYSTEM` in `code.py`): a synchronous
nested tool loop (up to 30 rounds, five filesystem tools only) with an
isolated `messages[]` and its own system prompt, returning only the last
assistant text to the parent. It is traced as `agent_create` /
`agent_start` … `agent_end` with `agent_kind="one_shot"`.

### Permission boundary

Layered authorization checked on the raw `tool_use` block before dispatch
(`permission_hook`, `DENY_LIST`, `safe_path` in `code.py`): `bash` commands
are screened against a substring deny list (`rm -rf /`, `sudo`, …) and then
require an interactive `Allow? [y/N]` answer (main thread only — asynchronous
turns fail closed); `read_file`/`write_file`/`edit_file` paths must resolve
inside `WORKDIR`; `mcp__*` tools follow their host policy. A string returned
by the PreToolUse hook short-circuits dispatch and becomes the denying
tool_result.

### Plan gate

Per-teammate approval state (`plan_gates`, manipulated by
`spawn_teammate_thread`, `_teammate_submit_plan`, `_run_teammate_tool`,
`complete_task`, and `advance_assignment_version` in `code.py`): values
`required`/`pending`/`approved`/`rejected`/`not_required` hard-block
`bash`, `write_file`, and `edit_file` (in `_run_teammate_tool`) and
`complete_task` until the lead approves a submitted plan.
`advance_assignment_version` re-arms the gate to `required` whenever a new
assignment is claimed, so old approvals never leak into new work.

### Prompt assembly

`assemble_system_prompt` + `PROMPT_SECTIONS` in `code.py`: the system prompt
is rebuilt from live context **every turn** in fixed section order
(identity, tools, tasks, teams, workspace, memory, compaction), followed by
the current time, the skills catalog, and — when present — the memory
catalog, relevant memory records, and connected MCP servers, joined by blank
lines.

### Skill catalog

`skills/<name>/SKILL.md` packages (YAML frontmatter `name`/`description`)
scanned at startup into `SKILL_REGISTRY` by `scan_skills` (`code.py`). Only
the name-plus-description catalog (`list_skills`) enters the system prompt;
full skill content is fetched on demand through the `load_skill` tool.

### Summary stats

`trace_stats.py` (`validate_file`, `Aggregate.add_file`, `main`): a
read-only, directory-wide consumer of `traces/*.jsonl` that first validates
every line against the trace envelope (required fields, string `event`,
object `data`; warnings for schema drift, `run_id` changes, missing
`run_start`/`run_end`), then aggregates model calls/models, stop reasons,
token totals from `model_response` usage, tool-name frequency, and
error/retry counts. Exit code 1 if any malformed line is found.

### Task board

Cross-session, dependency-aware task records under `.tasks/task_*.json`
(`Task`, `create_task`, `update_task`, `claim_task`, `complete_task` in
`code.py`), protected by an in-process `RLock` plus a cross-process `flock`
and atomic tmp+rename writes. `update_task` adds `blockedBy` edges only while
a task is pending and unowned (rejecting self-dependencies, missing targets,
and cycles via `_task_depends_on`); `claim_task` atomically verifies all
blockers (`can_start`), sets the owner and `in_progress`, and binds the
owner's cwd lease; `complete_task` requires ownership and a cleared plan gate.

### Teammate

A persistent teammate agent in its own daemon thread (`teammate-<name>`,
created by `spawn_teammate_thread` in `code.py`) with a reduced tool pool
(five filesystem tools plus `send_message`, `submit_plan`, `list_tasks`,
`claim_task`, `complete_task`) and a `MessageBus` inbox. Its filesystem tools
resolve cwd through `assignment_cwd` and fail closed until a task is claimed;
its final text is delivered to the lead as a `result` message, and when idle
it waits on the bus before auto-claiming the next ready task via
`claim_next_task`.

### Tool dispatch

The per-`tool_use`-block sequence in `agent_loop` (`code.py`): the `compact`
special case, then `PreToolUse` hooks (which can deny), then background
dispatch for marked bash calls, then the handler inside a
`tool_execution_start`/`tool_execution_end` span via `call_tool_handler`,
followed by `PostToolUse` hooks. All results — plus any newly finished
background notifications — are collected and appended as a single user
message by `build_user_content`.

### Trace event

One JSON object per line in a `traces/run_*.jsonl` file, emitted by
`TraceRecorder.emit` in `trace_runtime.py` with a fixed envelope: schema
version 1.0, UTC timestamp, `monotonic_ns`, `elapsed_ms`, `run_id`, `turn_id`,
`event_id`, `event`, agent identity fields, `span_id`/`parent_span_id`,
causal fields, thread info, and redacted `data`. The file is opened mode 0600,
appended line-buffered, and flushed per event; harness examples include
`harness_decision`, `context_compact`, `cron_*`, `task_*`, `background_*`, and
`model_retry`.

### Trace runtime

The harness-independent tracing library in `trace_runtime.py`
(`BaseTraceRecorder`, `NullTraceRecorder`, `TraceRecorder`,
`create_recorder`, `TracedClient`) plus `initialize_tracing` in `code.py`:
`NullTraceRecorder` is the default so importing the lesson never creates
files, while the CLI entry point creates a `TraceRecorder` from the
`HARNESS_TRACE*` environment variables. `wrap_client` turns every
`messages.create` into a `model_request` → `model_response`/`model_error`
span; `contextvars` scopes (turn, agent, model purpose, span) with
`capture_context`/`restore_context` keep worker-thread events attributable;
and `span()` pairs start/end events by `span_id`, recording `duration_ms` and
capturing exceptions as error data.

### Worktree (task-bound)

A real Git worktree under `.worktrees/<name>` on branch `wt/<name>`, bound to
exactly one pending, unowned task after name, Git, and registry validation
(`create_worktree` in `code.py`). Claiming that task makes the worktree the
owner's cwd — `assignment_cwd`/`task_worktree_cwd` fail closed on broken
bindings — and removal stays host-owned (`remove_worktree`): it requires a
completed bound task, no active cwd leases or running background commands, and
